cover.title: 50 API Interview Questions
cover.subtitle: Backend / SDE Q&A Bank
cover.tagline: The 50 most asked API questions, with short answers and a visual on every page. Built for backend and SDE interview prep.

blocks.q: Q1. What is a REST API and what are its constraints?
a_bullets: A ==REST== API is an architectural style where clients act on named resources over HTTP, following six constraints.
Client-server, **stateless**, cacheable, uniform interface
Layered system; code on demand is optional
Resources are nouns: `/users/42`, not `/getUser`

blocks.q: Q2. What does it mean for an API to be stateless?
a_bullets: The server keeps ==no client session== between requests, so every request carries everything needed to process it.
Auth token, IDs and params travel with **each** call
Any server can answer, so scaling is just adding nodes
Cost: slightly bigger requests, no server-side memory

blocks.q: Q3. What is the difference between REST and SOAP?
a_bullets: REST is a lightweight ==style== using plain HTTP and usually JSON; SOAP is a strict ==protocol== wrapping everything in XML envelopes.
SOAP has a formal WSDL contract and built-in WS-Security
REST is lighter, cacheable and the default for web APIs
SOAP survives in banking and legacy enterprise systems

blocks.q: Q4. What is the difference between REST and GraphQL?
a_bullets: REST exposes many fixed resource URLs; ==GraphQL== exposes one endpoint where the client picks exactly the fields it wants.
GraphQL fixes over-fetching and many round trips
REST gets HTTP caching for free; GraphQL needs custom caching
GraphQL costs more: query complexity limits, harder monitoring

items: Pick **REST** for public, cacheable, resource-style APIs
Pick ==GraphQL== for varied clients needing different fields
Pick **SOAP** only when a legacy partner demands it

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: REST = resources + HTTP + six constraints. Stateless means every request is self-contained. SOAP is a strict XML protocol; GraphQL is client-shaped queries on one endpoint.

blocks.q: Q5. What is the difference between GET and POST?
a_bullets: ==GET== reads a resource without changing it, while ==POST== sends a body to make the server do something.
GET is safe, cacheable and bookmarkable
POST is not cached and changes server state
Never put secrets in a GET query string

blocks.q: Q6. What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
a_bullets: ==PUT== replaces the whole resource, while ==PATCH== changes only the fields you send.
PUT with a missing field resets it
PATCH sends a small diff, saving bandwidth
PUT is idempotent; PATCH may not be

blocks.q: Q7. Which HTTP methods are idempotent and which are safe?
a_bullets: A ==safe== method never changes server state; an ==idempotent== one gives the same end state when repeated.
Every safe method is also idempotent
DELETE is idempotent but not safe
POST is neither, so blind retries can duplicate

blocks.q: Q8. What is the difference between PUT and POST for creating a resource?
a_bullets: Use ==PUT== when the client picks the URL, and ==POST== when the server assigns the id.
PUT repeated is harmless: same URL, same state
POST repeated creates a duplicate each time
POST replies 201 with a Location header

items: Safe to auto-retry: **GET**, HEAD, PUT, DELETE
POST needs an ==Idempotency-Key== before any retry
OPTIONS and HEAD are safe too, used for metadata

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Safe means read-only. Idempotent means retry-proof. PUT replaces, PATCH edits, POST creates and is the one that is never safe to retry blindly.

blocks.q: Q9. What is the difference between 200, 201 and 204?
a_bullets: All three mean success, but they differ in what the body carries.
==200 OK==: success with a response body
==201 Created==: new resource made, send a Location header
==204 No Content==: success, nothing to return

blocks.q: Q10. What is the difference between 401 and 403?
a_bullets: 401 means the server does not know who you are; 403 means it knows and refuses.
**401** Unauthorized really means unauthenticated
Fix a 401 by logging in or refreshing the token
**403**: valid identity, but no permission for this action

blocks.q: Q11. When do you return 400 vs 422?
a_bullets: 400 means the request could not be understood; 422 means it was understood but invalid.
==400==: malformed syntax, such as broken JSON
==422==: well-formed, but a field or business rule fails
Many APIs use 400 for both; stay consistent

blocks.q: Q12. What do 429, 502, 503 and 504 mean?
a_bullets: 429 blames the client for sending too much; 502, 503 and 504 are server-side failures.
**429**: slow down, and honour the Retry-After header
**502** bad reply from upstream; **504** upstream too slow
**503**: overloaded or in maintenance, so retry later

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Pick the code that tells the client who must act: 4xx means fix the request, 5xx means the server owns it. Retry 429, 503 and 504 with backoff, never a 400, 401 or 403.

blocks.q: Q13. What is a JWT and how is it structured?
a_bullets: A ==JWT== is a signed, self-contained token the server verifies without a lookup.
Three Base64URL parts: header (algorithm, type), payload (claims)
Signature proves it was not tampered with

blocks.q: Q14. How does JWT authentication differ from session-based authentication?
a_bullets: A session keeps state on the server; a JWT keeps it in the **token**.
Session: random ID looked up in store
JWT: verify signature, no lookup; hard to revoke before expiry

blocks.q: Q15. Where should you store a JWT: localStorage or an HttpOnly cookie?
a_bullets: Prefer an ==HttpOnly== cookie: JavaScript cannot read it, so XSS cannot steal it.
localStorage: any XSS script can read it
Cookie needs `Secure` and `SameSite`; CSRF risk, so add a token

blocks.q: Q16. How do you revoke a JWT and handle refresh tokens?
a_bullets: Keep access tokens short-lived; store a revocable refresh token server-side.
Access token: 5-15 minutes; rotate refresh token on every use
Denylist a token's `jti` until it expires
A JWT is signed, not secret: short expiry, rotating refresh, HttpOnly cookies

blocks.q: Q17. What is OAuth 2.0 and what problem does it solve?
a_bullets: OAuth 2.0 lets an app get ==limited access== to a user's data on another service **without** ever seeing their password.
The user approves scopes like `read:photos`
The app receives a short-lived access token
Revoke the token, not the password

blocks.q: Q18. What is the difference between OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect?
a_bullets: OAuth 2.0 handles ==authorization== (what you may access); OpenID Connect adds **authentication** (who you are) on top.
OIDC adds an ID token, a signed JWT
Request it with the `openid` scope
UserInfo endpoint returns profile claims

blocks.q: Q19. How does the Authorization Code flow with PKCE work?
a_bullets: The app proves it started the flow by sending a ==code_verifier== hash first, then the raw verifier when swapping the code.
Challenge is `SHA256(verifier)`, base64url-encoded
A stolen code is useless without the verifier
Required for SPAs and mobile apps

blocks.q: Q20. What is the difference between the Authorization Code and Client Credentials grants?
a_bullets: Authorization Code acts on behalf of a ==user==; Client Credentials is **machine-to-machine** with no user involved.
Code flow: user consent, redirect, user-scoped token
Client Credentials: client ID and secret for a token
Use it for cron jobs and service calls

blocks.title: Scope tip
blocks.text: Request the least scopes you need; users trust narrow consent screens.

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: OAuth 2.0 delegates access, OIDC proves identity, and PKCE secures public clients.

blocks.q: Q21. What is CORS and why does the browser block cross-origin requests?
a_bullets: CORS is a browser-enforced ==opt-in== that lets a server allow other origins to read its responses, relaxing the same-origin policy.
Origin = scheme + host + port; any difference is cross-origin
The server opts in with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`
Blocking protects users: **sites** can't read your bank's data

blocks.q: Q22. What is a preflight request and when is it sent?
a_bullets: A preflight is an automatic ==OPTIONS== request the browser sends first to ask permission before a risky cross-origin call.
Sent for PUT/DELETE, custom headers or JSON content type
Simple GET/POST with basic headers skip it
Cache the answer with `Access-Control-Max-Age`

blocks.q: Q23. What is the difference between CSRF and XSS, and how do you stop each?
a_bullets: **CSRF** tricks a logged-in browser into sending a forged request; ==XSS== injects script that runs inside your site.
CSRF: SameSite cookies plus anti-CSRF tokens
XSS: escape output, set a CSP, avoid innerHTML
HttpOnly cookies limit what stolen scripts can read

blocks.q: Q24. What is BOLA/IDOR and how do you prevent it?
a_bullets: ==BOLA== (IDOR) means an API returns an object by ID without checking the caller owns it.
Check ownership on **every** object access, server-side
Use the token's user, never a client-sent user ID
Random UUIDs help, but are not authorization
example_code: // user A reads user B's order

blocks.title: CORS tip
blocks.text: Allowlist exact origins; `*` cannot be combined with credentials, and never echo Origin blindly.

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: CORS is browser-only, not server security. Preflight asks first. Stop CSRF with SameSite tokens, XSS with escaping, BOLA with ownership checks.

blocks.q: Q25. What is the difference between offset and cursor pagination?
a_bullets: ==Offset== skips N rows by position; ==cursor== resumes after the last row you saw.
Offset: simple, allows jumping to page 50
Offset drifts when rows are inserted or deleted
Cursor: stable and fast, but no random page jump

blocks.q: Q26. Why is offset pagination slow on large tables?
a_bullets: The database must **scan and discard** every skipped row before returning yours.
OFFSET 1000000 reads a million rows first
Cost grows linearly with page depth
Keyset `WHERE id < ?` uses the index directly

blocks.q: Q27. How do you design filtering and sorting query parameters?
a_bullets: Use plain, ==whitelisted== query params: field filters, one `sort` param, a `-` prefix for descending.
Whitelist sortable and filterable fields
Add a unique tiebreaker like `id` to every sort
Back common filters with composite indexes

blocks.q: Q28. How do you paginate a feed where new items keep arriving?
a_bullets: Use ==cursor (keyset)== pagination so new items at the top never shift your position.
Cursor anchors to a row, not a page number
Order by `(created_at, id)` for a stable cursor
Return `next_cursor` and fetch new items separately

blocks.title: Limit tip
blocks.text: Set a default `limit` and cap it (say 100), so no client can request a million rows.

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Offset is simple but slow and drifts; use cursor for big or live feeds, and always whitelist sort fields with a unique tiebreaker.

blocks.q: Q29. What is rate limiting and why do APIs need it?
a_bullets: It caps how many requests a client may send in a time window, so ==no single caller== can starve the rest.
Stops abuse, brute-force and scraping
Keeps costs and latency predictable
Over the limit returns `429` + `Retry-After`

blocks.q: Q30. How does the token bucket algorithm work?
a_bullets: A bucket refills with **tokens** at a fixed rate, and each request spends one token or is rejected.
Capacity sets the allowed burst size
Refill rate sets the long-run average
Empty bucket means 429 until refill

blocks.q: Q31. What is the difference between fixed window, sliding window and leaky bucket?
a_bullets: They differ in how they ==count== requests over time, trading accuracy, memory and burst handling.
Fixed window can allow 2x burst at the edge
Sliding window is smoother but costs more memory
Leaky bucket drains at a steady rate

blocks.title: Limit key tip
blocks.text: Key limits by API key or user ID, not just IP; one shared NAT can block a whole office.

blocks.q: Q32. How do you implement distributed rate limiting across servers?
a_bullets: Keep the counters in one ==shared store== such as Redis, so every server sees the same count.
Update atomically with INCR or a Lua script
Set a TTL so old windows expire
Decide to fail open or closed if Redis is down

blocks.title: Fail open or closed?
blocks.text: Fail open for public reads to stay up; fail closed for login and payments to stay safe.

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Limit per client key, return 429 with Retry-After, and keep the counters in shared Redis.

blocks.q: Q33. How does HTTP caching work with Cache-Control and ETag?
a_bullets: `Cache-Control` sets how long a response is ==fresh==, and an `ETag` lets the client revalidate it once stale.
`max-age=60` serves from cache with **no** request
Client resends the tag in `If-None-Match`
**304** means reuse the cached body

blocks.q: Q34. What is the difference between ETag and Last-Modified?
a_bullets: An ==ETag== is a content fingerprint, while `Last-Modified` is only a timestamp with 1-second resolution.
ETag catches edits within the same second
`Last-Modified` pairs with `If-Modified-Since`
When both are sent, **ETag** wins

blocks.q: Q35. How do you cache API responses in Redis and invalidate them?
a_bullets: Store the response under a key built from the request, give it a ==TTL==, and delete the key when data changes.
Key holds path, query and user scope
TTL caps staleness if an invalidation is missed
**Delete** on write rather than updating the entry

blocks.q: Q36. What is the difference between cache-aside, write-through and write-back?
a_bullets: The three differ in who fills the cache and when the database is written: the app on a miss, both together, or the cache first.
==Cache-aside==: app loads on miss, can serve stale data
==Write-through==: cache and DB together, slower writes
==Write-back==: **fastest** writes, but a crash loses data

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Use max-age for freshness and ETag for cheap revalidation. In Redis, set a TTL and delete on write. Pick the write strategy by how much staleness or loss you can accept.

blocks.q: Q37. What is a webhook and how does it differ from polling?
a_bullets: A webhook is an HTTP callback where the provider ==pushes== an event to your URL the moment it happens, instead of you asking repeatedly.
Polling wastes calls and adds up to one interval of delay
Webhook is event-driven: near real-time, one request per event
Your endpoint must be public and answer fast with 2xx

blocks.q: Q38. How do you make webhook delivery secure and reliable?
a_bullets: Sign every payload with a shared secret so receivers can verify it, and retry failed deliveries with backoff.
Verify the {red:HMAC} signature on the raw body, then check timestamp
Return 2xx fast; process async from a queue
Provider retries on non-2xx, so receivers must dedupe by event id

blocks.q: Q39. What is idempotency and how do you implement idempotency keys?
a_bullets: An operation is idempotent when repeating it has the same effect as doing it once, and an ==idempotency key== makes POST safe to retry.
Client sends a unique key (UUID) per logical operation
Server stores key with its response, replays it on retry
Same key with a different body returns 422

blocks.title: Key expiry tip
blocks.text: Keep stored idempotency keys for 24 hours, then expire them so the table stays small.

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Webhooks push events, so **sign** them and ack fast. Retries are guaranteed, so make every handler **idempotent**.

blocks.q: Q40. How do you version a REST API?
a_bullets: Put a version in the request so old clients keep working while new ones adopt changes.
==URI path== `/v1/` is the most common and easiest to route
Header or media type keeps URLs clean but is harder to test
Version only on breaking changes, not every release

blocks.q: Q41. What counts as a breaking change and how do you deprecate safely?
a_bullets: A change is ==breaking== if a correct existing client would fail or misbehave after it.
Removing or renaming a field, or changing its type
Adding a required parameter or tightening validation
Announce, add a Sunset date, monitor usage, then remove

rows: Change status code or error shape

caption.text:
50 API questions they will ask you in your backend/SDE interview 🎯

API rounds are where a lot of good candidates lose offers. So here are the 50 most asked questions, handwritten and broken into easy pages, 3-4 questions each, with short answers, key points and a visual.

What's covered:
📌 REST and HTTP fundamentals
📌 HTTP methods, safety and status codes
📌 JWT and session authentication
📌 OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect
📌 CORS and API security
📌 Pagination, filtering and sorting
📌 Rate limiting and throttling
📌 API caching
📌 Webhooks and idempotency
📌 Versioning and file uploads
📌 Gateways, testing and monitoring
📌 Scalability and real-world design scenarios
📌 A one-page cheatsheet to revise before you walk in

Save this so it's with you the night before the interview 🔖

Which API question do you find the hardest? OAuth flows, idempotency, rate limiting or the design scenarios? Tell us in the comments 👇

Comment “api” to get all the answers as a PDF.
